planting.note: Plant a rooted crown, sucker, or slip after the last frost in fast-draining soil in full sun, or grow in a large container moved under cover for winter.

directions: MD2 was selected from Pineapple Research Institute of Hawaii breeding stock and later commercialized by Del Monte in Costa Rica in 1996, where it quickly displaced Smooth Cayenne as the dominant fresh-market pineapple worldwide because of its high sugar content, low acidity, amber rind at ripeness, and much better cold-storage life for shipping. Plant a rooted crown or sucker in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; fruiting typically takes 18-24 months from planting under warm conditions. The golden-fleshed fruit holds its sweetness and shelf quality far longer after harvest than older cultivars, which is why it became the standard supermarket pineapple. Protect from frost and water moderately, letting the soil dry between waterings since the plant stores water in its leaf bases.
sources: USDA ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository

planting.note: Plant a rooted crown or slip after the last frost in fast-draining soil in full to mostly-full sun.

directions: Sugarloaf is a cylindrical, white-fleshed pineapple grown widely in Hawaii, the Philippines, and Costa Rica, prized as one of the sweetest and lowest-acid pineapples available with a tender, nearly non-fibrous edible core. Its thin rind and delicate flesh make it ship poorly, which is why it stays mostly a backyard and farmers-market fruit rather than a commercial export like MD2 or Smooth Cayenne. The smooth-edged leaves carry a pink blush down the center and the plant stays compact, suiting containers as well as ground planting in warm climates. Grow in gritty, well-drained soil and allow the soil to dry between waterings; harvest when the shell turns from green toward pale gold for peak sweetness.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree after danger of frost has passed in full sun on well-drained soil; grafted trees fruit in 4-6 years versus 10+ for seedlings.

directions: Si Thong, meaning 'golden,' is one of the premier named sweet-tamarind cultivars developed in Thailand, selected for large, thick-fleshed pods with mild, low-acid pulp sweet enough to eat fresh like a candied date rather than being reserved for the tart cooking pulp of seedling tamarinds. The tree needs a long hot growing season and tolerates drought and poor soil once established, but is sensitive to frost and waterlogging. Grafted trees bear considerably sooner and truer to type than seedling-grown tamarinds, and pods are typically left to dry fully on the tree before harvest to concentrate their sugars. Give it full sun and deep, well-drained soil, and expect a large, long-lived shade tree in addition to its fruit crop.

planting.note: Transplant after all frost danger has passed; seed loses viability quickly and should be sown fresh.

directions: Pacay is the highland Andean counterpart to the lowland Amazonian ice-cream bean (Inga edulis), long cultivated in the mountain valleys and coastal regions of Peru and Ecuador where Incan traders once carried its pods to Cuzco. Long, often twisted pods contain seeds wrapped in a soft, cottony white pulp that tastes mildly sweet and vanilla-like, eaten fresh out of hand rather than cooked. As a nitrogen-fixing legume tree it tolerates poorer soils and is commonly planted as a shade or street tree in addition to its fruit crop, and it handles cooler highland temperatures better than most tropical Inga species. Plant in full sun with regular moisture while young, and expect a large, fast-growing tree that needs ample room to spread.
sources: growables.org Tropical Fruit Database (Univ. of Florida)

planting.note: Transplant into a sheltered, shaded or part-shaded rainforest-margin position after frost danger passes.

directions: Smooth Davidson's plum is a rare understory rainforest tree from the subtropical lowlands of northeastern New South Wales and southeastern Queensland, differing from the better-known Davidsonia pruriens by its hairless, glossy leaves and stems. Deep burgundy fruits hang in clusters directly on the trunk and branches and are intensely tart, used mainly cooked into jams, sauces, and cordials rather than eaten fresh. In the wild it survives in only a handful of scattered populations, but it is increasingly grown in native bush-food plantings and home gardens for its ornamental foliage and reliable fruit set under cultivation. Give it a humid, part-shaded site with rich, moisture-retentive soil protected from wind and frost, mimicking its native rainforest-margin habitat.
sources: NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water — Threatened Species Profile

planting.note: Root a stem cutting or transplant a container-grown plant after frost danger passes in full sun on gritty, fast-draining soil.

directions: Pitayo de mayo is a tree-like columnar cactus long cultivated on small farms in the Sayula Basin of Jalisco, Mexico, grown for its sweet, brightly colored early-spring fruit that ripens before most other pitaya species. Plants are usually propagated from cuttings of selected high-fruiting clones rather than seed, since named selections are reliably true to type and fruit years sooner than seedlings. It thrives in rocky, low-fertility, semiarid ground with minimal irrigation once established, and its arborescent branching habit eventually forms a small multi-trunked tree. Give it full sun and sharply drained soil, and protect young plants from frost since mature plants have only modest cold tolerance.
sources: ResearchGate: Ethnobotany, Productivity, and Ecophysiology of Pitaya (Stenocereus queretaroensis)
